style_2_guidelines.guideline_authority: IDSA International Clinical Practice Guidelines for the Treatment of Acute Uncomplicated Cystitis
pearls: Ineffective if eGFR < 30 mL/min (insufficient urinary concentration and risk of peripheral neuropathy). Ineffective for pyelonephritis.
High urinary concentration sustained over 48 hours. Lower clinical cure rate than 5-day nitrofurantoin.
Avoid Ampicillin or Amoxicillin monotherapy due to very high worldwide E. coli resistance.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Do not use Nitrofurantoin if eGFR < 30 mL/min.
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Asymptomatic bacteriuria in pregnancy MUST be treated. Safe choices: Nitrofurantoin (avoid near term weeks 38–42 due to neonatal hemolysis), Amoxicillin/Clavulanate, or Cephalexin.

style_3_monograph.summary: The urinary system is the body's drainage system for removing wastes and extra water. It includes two kidneys, two ureters, a bladder, and a urethra. Urinary tract infections (UTIs) are the second most common type of infection in the body. You may have a UTI if you notice: Pain or burning when you urinate Fever, tiredness, or shakiness An urge to urinate often Pressure in your lower belly Urine that smells bad or looks cloudy or reddish Pain in your back or side below the ribs People of any age or sex can get UTIs. But about four times as many women get UTIs as men. You're also at higher risk if you have diabetes, need a tube to drain your bladder, or have a spinal cord injury. If you think you have a UTI it is important to see your doctor. Your doctor can tell if you have a UTI with a urine test . Treatment is with antibiotics. NIH: National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases
style_3_monograph.treatment: Most people who have bacteria growing in their urine, but no symptoms, do not need treatment. This is because the bacteria are not causing any harm. In fact, treating people with this problem may make it harder to treat infections in the future. However, for some people getting a urinary tract infection may cause more severe problems. As a result, treatment with antibiotics may be needed if: You are pregnant. You recently had a kidney transplant. You are scheduled for surgery involving the prostate gland or the bladder. You have kidney stones that have caused an infection. Your young child has urinary reflux (backward movement of urine from the bladder into ureters or kidneys). Without symptoms being present, even people who are older adults, have diabetes, or have a catheter in place do not need treatment.
